title: Is Porsche Bringing the Flat-Eight Back?
excerpt: Reports point to a new Porsche halo car, internally called the S1, with a flat-eight engine. And Porsche has already built and tested one.
body: Porsche may be preparing something very interesting for its next halo car.
Recent reports suggest the company is considering a new flagship sports car, reportedly known internally as the **S1**, and one detail in particular has caught our attention: **a flat-eight engine.**
For a company so closely associated with the flat-six, that would be a pretty significant move. And the interesting part is that Porsche has already built one.
## Porsche Has Already Built a Flat-Eight
This is not simply an internet rumor. Porsche previously developed a 5.0-liter twin-turbocharged flat-eight for a proposed mid-engine supercar project. The reported figures are impressive:

- 5.0-liter displacement
- Twin turbochargers
- Approximately 750 horsepower
- Approximately 1,000 Nm of torque
- 9,000 RPM redline
- Manual transmission

More importantly, **Porsche actually tested the engine.** The flat-eight was installed into a modified Cayman test car and driven around Porsche's Weissach development facility. The project reportedly continued for more than a year before eventually being cancelled.
So while the production car never happened, Porsche already has experience developing and testing a modern, high-output flat-eight. That makes the current rumors considerably more interesting.
## Porsche Has a History With Flat-Eights
The flat-eight is not new territory for Porsche. The company has used horizontally opposed eight-cylinder engines in motorsport, most notably with the Porsche 908.

What Porsche has never done, however, is put a flat-eight into a regular production road car. That is what could make the rumored S1 so significant. If Porsche actually moves forward with a production flat-eight, it would be the first time the configuration reaches a Porsche road car.
## What About the Carrera GT?
The Carrera GT is an important part of this story, but it is worth clearing up one common misconception: **the Carrera GT did not use a flat-eight.**

It was powered by a 5.7-liter naturally aspirated V8 producing 603 horsepower, paired with a six-speed manual transmission. The engine was derived from Porsche's motorsport development work and became one of the defining features of the car. The 918 Spyder followed with another naturally aspirated V8, this time combined with a hybrid system and all-wheel drive.

A new flat-eight-powered Porsche would therefore represent something different from both cars. Rather than simply bringing back an old engine, Porsche would be introducing an entirely new production engine configuration to its modern road-car lineup.
## Why a Flat-Eight?

There are some obvious reasons Porsche could be interested in the configuration. A boxer engine keeps the center of gravity low, while adding two cylinders creates the potential for more displacement and power without moving away from Porsche's horizontally opposed architecture.

But there is also the character of the engine itself. A high-revving flat-eight would have a very different personality from the turbocharged V8s and hybrid powertrains becoming increasingly common in modern supercars.
And Porsche already knows what its prototype can do. The previously developed engine reportedly reached 9,000 RPM, which is remarkable for a twin-turbocharged eight-cylinder.
## There Is Still a Lot We Don't Know

This is where it is important to separate the confirmed history from the current speculation. Porsche's previous flat-eight prototype is well documented. The rumored S1, however, has not been fully revealed by Porsche, and there is no confirmation that the previously developed 5.0-liter engine is the exact engine that would be used in a future production car.
The reports surrounding the project are still developing, so we should treat the current specifications as exactly what they are: **reports, not confirmed production specifications.**
## But It Is Hard Not to Get Excited
If Porsche does move forward with a flat-eight-powered halo car, it could be one of the most interesting combustion-engine projects we've seen from the company in years.

Imagine a mid-engine Porsche with a high-revving flat-eight, serious turbocharged power, a lightweight chassis and potentially a manual transmission. That would be quite a statement in an industry moving rapidly toward electrification.

Porsche has already shown that the technology is possible. They built the engine. They put it in a car. They tested it. Now the question is whether Porsche is finally ready to give that engine a production home.

For now, we will have to wait for Porsche to make it official. But if the rumors are accurate, the next Porsche halo car could be something very special. And at Performance Connect, **we will definitely be watching.**
sourceNote: Based on industry reports. Porsche has not officially confirmed the S1 or its powertrain.

title: Honda's Civic Type R Survives in America — But Its Future Might Not Include a Manual
excerpt: Honda just confirmed the 2026 Civic Type R keeps its spot in American showrooms. But Europe already said goodbye, and rumors are building about what comes next.
body: Honda just confirmed the 2026 Civic Type R will keep its spot in American showrooms — for now. But the news isn't all good, and it comes wrapped in a bigger story about where Honda's hot hatch is headed next.

**The good news first.** While speculation swirled that the Type R could disappear from the US lineup, Honda quietly put that to rest by releasing 2026 pricing: $46,895 before destination, $48,090 with it. That's another price bump, but the car itself is unchanged — still the 315-horsepower, 2.0-liter turbo-four, still backed by a 6-speed manual, still front-wheel drive only. This is the same car that set the FWD record at the Nurburgring at 7:44.881, so "unchanged" here means "still one of the best front-drive cars money can buy."

**Europe didn't get the same news.** Back in June, Honda confirmed the Type R is being discontinued across Europe, marking the send-off with a 40-unit "Ultimate Edition" — pearl white paint, black roof, red decals, carbon-fiber rear wing and sill plates. Only 10 of those 40 are headed to the UK. The reasoning is mostly regulatory: European emissions targets are squeezing out higher-polluting performance models across the industry, and the Type R isn't the only one feeling it.

**Here's the part that should actually worry Type R fans.** Honda hasn't confirmed anything officially, but there's real speculation building that the next-generation Civic Type R could borrow a more powerful version of the hybrid powertrain debuting in the revived Honda Prelude — complete with the Prelude's S+ Shift system that simulates gear changes rather than using a real manual gearbox. If that happens, the current FL5-generation Type R could go down as the last manual, non-hybrid version of the car ever made.

For now, the manual Type R is still here, still naturally — well, turbocharged — exciting, and still buyable in the US. If you've been on the fence, the writing might be on the wall for how long that lasts.
sourceNote: Sources: Honda Civic Type R 2026 US pricing announcement; Honda Europe Civic Type R Ultimate Edition release.
